name: Design an A/B Experimentation Platform
intent: Split users into groups the same way every time, record who actually saw what, turn raw events into metrics, and decide with honest statistics when a change helped, hurt or made no difference.
prompt: Design an experimentation platform for a product with 50 million daily users. Teams run hundreds of experiments at once, such as a new checkout page or a changed ranking. Each user must always see the same variant. The platform must measure the effect on business metrics, tell teams when a result can be trusted, stop an experiment that is hurting users, and let a change roll out gradually.
codeTitle: hash bucketing, ramp-ups, layers and an honest significance test
finalIntro: One user landing on a new checkout page, from assignment to a trustworthy result.
functional: Assign each user to a variant of an experiment, the same one every time
Log an exposure when the user actually sees the variant
Compute metrics per variant from the product's event stream
Report the effect size, a confidence interval and whether it is significant
Estimate the sample size and the duration before an experiment starts
Ramp an experiment from a small share of users to everyone, and turn it off at once
Run many experiments at the same time without them contaminating each other
nonFunctional: Assignment adds under 1 ms and works even when the platform is down (fall back to control)
Handle about 100,000 assignment checks per second at the peak, and billions of events per day
Results are fresh within an hour, and final results are exactly reproducible from the raw events
A bad experiment is detected and stopped within minutes, not days
The false positive rate matches what the report claims, even when people look at results daily
Every decision can be audited: who changed what, and which data produced the result

firstAttempt.text: The app flips a coin on each request: if random() is below 0.5 it shows the new page, otherwise the old one. It writes a variant column on the events it already sends to the main database. An analyst runs a SQL query at the end of the week, compares the average conversion of both groups, and looks at the p-value in a spreadsheet. Whenever someone is curious, they run the query again.
limits: A user who reloads can see both pages, so no one has a stable experience and the groups are mixed
The variant is recorded for every request, including users who never reached the changed page, which dilutes the effect
Analytics queries on the production database are slow and slow the product down
Nobody knows how long to run it, so people stop when the number looks good, and that produces false wins
A broken variant keeps running until someone happens to notice
Two experiments on the same page silently change each other's results

steps.title: Assign users by hashing, not by coin flip
steps.problem: A random choice on every request gives the same user different experiences, and it cannot be reproduced later, so no one can say which group a person belonged to.
steps.fix: Make the assignment a pure function of the user and the experiment. Compute a hash such as FNV-1a or MurmurHash of the experiment's salt plus the user id, reduce it to a bucket from 0 to 9999, and map ranges of buckets to variants: below 5000 is treatment, the rest is control. The same input always gives the same answer, on any server, with no lookup and no stored state. The salt differs per experiment, so the groups of one experiment are unrelated to the groups of another. The assignment code ships as a small SDK that reads the experiment definitions from a config service and caches them locally, so a call takes microseconds and still works if the platform is down.
steps.tradeoff: Assignment is stable, fast and reproducible, and nothing has to be stored per user. The price is that the hash must be well mixed (a weak one skews the groups), the salt must never be reused, and changing the allocation of a running experiment moves users between groups and breaks it. Users who change identity, for example logged out and then logged in, can land in different groups.

steps.title: Log an exposure only when the user sees the variant
steps.problem: Being assigned is not the same as being affected. If the metric analysis includes users who were assigned but never opened the changed page, the real effect is diluted and the test needs far more users.
steps.fix: When the code actually renders the variant, the SDK emits an exposure event: user id, experiment, variant, a timestamp and the SDK version. Exposures and product events (clicks, purchases, page views) go onto a common event stream in the same format, keyed by user id. The analysis later counts only users with at least one exposure, from the time of their first exposure. Exposures are sent in batches and de-duplicated on an event id, because mobile apps retry and the same exposure may arrive twice.
steps.tradeoff: The analysis covers exactly the users who could have been affected, which sharpens the measurement. It adds event volume (one exposure per rendering, which the SDK throttles to the first one per session), and both arms must log exposure in the same way, otherwise a variant that logs more often looks like a different population.

steps.title: Turn events into metrics with a pipeline
steps.problem: Raw events are billions of rows per day. Running analytical queries on them in the production database is slow, and every team computes revenue per user a little differently.
steps.fix: Land every event in an append-only raw event store (columnar files partitioned by day) and also feed it to stream jobs. A pipeline joins each exposure to the later events of the same user, aggregates per user and per experiment (a sum of revenue, a count of orders, whether the user converted), and writes the result to a metric store with one row per user, experiment and metric. Metrics are defined once in a shared catalogue, with a name, a query and an owner. A stream job gives fresh numbers within the hour, and a nightly batch job recomputes the final numbers from the raw events and is the version that counts, since it also handles late events.
steps.tradeoff: Teams get one definition per metric, results do not depend on production load, and any number can be rebuilt from the raw data. The cost is a pipeline to operate, two paths (stream and batch) that must agree, and a delay: late events mean that today's number can still change tomorrow.

steps.title: Compute significance, and size the test in advance
steps.problem: A difference between two groups is partly luck. A team that stops when the numbers look good, or that runs a test too short to see a small effect, will ship noise.
steps.fix: A stats engine reads the per-user metrics and, for each metric, computes the mean of each arm, the difference, a confidence interval and a p-value from a z test (or a t test, or the delta method for ratios such as revenue per session). Before launch, the experiment form asks for the baseline rate, the smallest effect worth detecting and the traffic share, and calculates the sample size per arm, about 16 times the variance divided by the square of the effect, and from that the duration in whole weeks so that every weekday is covered. Two checks run on every result: a sample-ratio check, which compares the number of users per arm with the planned split using a chi-square test, because a mismatch means the assignment or the logging is broken and the result is void, and variance reduction (CUPED) which uses each user's behaviour before the test to cut the noise.
steps.tradeoff: Teams know up front how long a test must run and whether a result is credible. The honest answers are sometimes disappointing: small effects need weeks, and many experiments end as inconclusive. Running more metrics raises the chance that one of them looks significant by luck, so one primary metric is fixed in advance.

steps.title: Watch guardrails and handle peeking
steps.problem: Some experiments hurt users: they slow the page, raise crashes or cut revenue. And teams look at the dashboard every day, which, if the test is read as a fixed-sample test, turns a 5% false positive rate into 20% or more.
steps.fix: Every experiment declares guardrail metrics, such as page latency, error rate, crash rate and unsubscribes, that must not get worse. A guardrail monitor checks them every few minutes with sequential tests, whose boundaries are wider at the beginning and are valid at any time you look (for example an always-valid confidence sequence, or an alpha-spending plan with a fixed number of looks). If a guardrail crosses its boundary, the monitor tells the ramp controller to turn the experiment off and pages the owner. The success metric uses the same sequential method, so a team may check the result daily and stop early when the evidence is strong, without inflating false positives.
steps.tradeoff: A harmful change is stopped within minutes, and peeking becomes safe. Sequential boundaries are wider than a single-look test, so a real small effect takes somewhat longer to confirm, and guardrails with many metrics need a correction so that the monitor does not raise false alarms by itself.

steps.title: Run many experiments side by side and ramp up safely
steps.problem: Hundreds of experiments run at once. Two that change the same part of the product interact, and a new feature that is switched on for everyone at once can take the site down.
steps.fix: Group experiments into layers by the surface they touch (checkout, search ranking, notifications). Experiments in the same layer split the buckets between them, so a user is in at most one of them. Experiments in different layers use different salts, so they are statistically independent and each one sees a balanced mix of the other's variants, which means interactions average out. Experiments that are known to interact are put in the same layer or declared mutually exclusive. Rollouts go through a ramp controller: 1%, then 5%, 25%, 50% and 100%, with a hold at each stage to check the guardrails. Because the ramp is a threshold on a separate hash, users who were in at 1% are still in at 5%, and keep their variant.
steps.tradeoff: Teams can run many tests in parallel and ship gradually with a fast off switch. Layers reduce the traffic available to each experiment and need an owner who plans them, and a detected interaction between layers can only be studied after the fact, by analysing the cells jointly.

failures.scenario: Sample-ratio mismatch: the treatment arm has 3% fewer users than planned
failures.impact: The usual cause is that the new variant crashes or loads slowly, so some of its exposures are never logged. The users who are missing are not random, so the comparison is biased and any win is meaningless.
failures.answer: The stats engine runs a chi-square check on user counts for every experiment, and a failed check marks the result as invalid instead of showing the numbers. The owner investigates the logging and the assignment path before the experiment is restarted with a new salt.

failures.scenario: The assignment service is down or the config cannot be fetched
failures.impact: If every call depended on the service, the product itself would be unavailable, and the missing users would also distort every running experiment.
failures.answer: The SDK evaluates assignment locally from a cached config and never calls the platform per request. If the config is stale or missing, it serves the control variant and logs no exposure, so the product works, and the analysis simply excludes those users. A health check and a config version in each exposure make a stale fleet visible.

failures.scenario: Late and duplicate events arrive from mobile apps
failures.impact: A phone that was offline sends yesterday's purchases today. A naive stream job misses them, and a retry may count the same purchase twice, so metrics move after being reported.
failures.answer: Every event carries a unique id and the jobs de-duplicate on it. Streaming jobs use event time and a watermark with an allowed lateness, and the nightly batch recomputes the day from the raw events, which is the number the final report uses. Dashboards say how complete a day is.

failures.scenario: A team peeks every day and ships the first significant result
failures.impact: With a fixed-sample test, checking daily for a month gives a false win in roughly one A/A test in four, so the company slowly fills with changes that do nothing.
failures.answer: The platform uses sequential tests whose boundaries are valid at every look, shows the planned sample size and progress, and marks a result as final only when the planned size or the boundary is reached. A periodic A/A test of the whole pipeline checks that the false positive rate really is about 5%.

failures.scenario: The same user appears in several accounts or devices
failures.impact: A user who browses logged out on a phone and buys logged in on a laptop is two ids with two buckets, so they may see both variants, and their purchase is not linked to the exposure.
failures.answer: Pick the unit of randomisation to match the unit of the metric: a stable account id for logged-in features, a device id for anonymous ones. For pages used before and after login, bucket on the device id and join identities in the pipeline afterwards, and monitor the share of users with conflicting variants.

alternatives.title: How to assign users

options.name: Hash of salt and user id
options.pro: Stateless, stable, reproducible and microseconds fast
options.con: Cannot easily move a user, and a poor hash or reused salt skews the groups

options.name: Random draw stored per user
options.pro: Any allocation is possible, and users can be moved
options.con: A stored mapping to read on every request and to keep in sync

options.name: Random choice per request
options.con: Unstable experience, and no way to analyse by user

alternatives.pick: A hash of an experiment salt and the user id, evaluated locally by the SDK.

alternatives.title: Fixed-sample or sequential testing

options.name: Fixed-sample z test
options.pro: Simple, familiar and the most powerful for one look at the end
options.con: Invalid if anyone looks early, which they will

options.name: Sequential or always-valid tests
options.pro: Safe to monitor continuously, and allows early stops
options.con: Wider intervals, and harder to explain

options.name: Bayesian with a posterior probability
options.pro: Gives an intuitive probability that B beats A
options.con: Stopping rules and priors still matter, and the false positive rate is not guaranteed by default

alternatives.pick: Sequential tests for guardrails and for monitoring, and a pre-registered sample size for the headline decision.

alternatives.title: Where overlapping experiments live

options.name: Everything independent with different salts
options.con: Interactions between related changes remain hidden

options.name: Layers with disjoint buckets
options.pro: No overlap within a layer, so no interaction there
options.con: Each experiment gets only part of the traffic in its layer

options.name: Full factorial design
options.con: The number of cells multiplies, so it is rarely affordable

alternatives.pick: Independent layers by surface, with exclusion inside a layer for experiments that are known to interact.

alternatives.title: How fresh the metrics are

options.name: Nightly batch only
options.con: A bad variant runs for hours before anyone notices

options.name: Stream processing only
options.con: Late events and bugs change the numbers, and state is expensive

options.name: Stream for guardrails, batch for the final numbers
options.pro: Fast safety checks and a clean final answer
options.con: Two code paths that must be kept consistent

alternatives.pick: Stream for guardrails and live monitoring, nightly batch from the raw events for the official result.
